title: Audit skewers Maryland Department of the Environment lease, among others
summary: Auditors panned a $167.1 million lease deal for the Maryland Department of the Environment in a report released Thursday afternoon, arguing the state overpaid to secure a $10 million office renovation budget from its landlord.
content:
by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters July 31, 2025

by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters July 31, 2025

Auditors panned a $167.1 million lease deal for the Maryland Department of the Environment in a report released Thursday afternoon, arguing the state overpaid to secure a $10 million office renovation budget from its landlord.

The Department of the Environment lease was one of several that auditors determined could not be justified by the Maryland Department of General Services — which handles state leasing — including $410.9 million worth of leases to relocate state agencies to offices in downtown Baltimore. The Moore administration had upheld the Baltimore deals as a cost savings.

The audit, previously reported by Maryland Matters, pointed to several “questionable” aspects of the Department of the Environment’s lease, including its 20-year term, a 3.45% annual cost escalation and the omission of a key termination right for the state.

Auditors wrote that the $10 million renovation may have skirted state budget law, after General Services revealed that it pursued the strategy in part because the environmental agency didn’t have the budget for renovations to its offices.

Auditors wrote that, because of an elevated rental cost, the state would be paying an extra $12.6 million, essentially funding the largely cosmetic renovations to privately held Montgomery Park, a converted warehouse building in West Baltimore along Interstate 95.

They argued the agreement was out of the ordinary in “numerous aspects,” and cast doubt on whether it was in the best interest of the state’s finances. Meanwhile, state government is in the midst of a historic budget pinch, with an effort to slash payrolls through a $20,000 buyout offer to employees, and to axe real estate costs wherever possible.

The Department of General Services disputed many of the audit’s findings, and argued that the lease actually saved the state money, because the escalation rate decreased compared to the 4% escalator in the previous lease at Montgomery Park, where the environmental agency has been since 2002.

The agency fiercely defended its strategy of rolling the renovation budget into the lease, arguing that the practice “allows the state to strategically leverage its buying power by having landlords design and construct leased space to the State’s exact specifications.”

In its response, the agency stated that the Department of the Environment was “unable to consider directly paying $10 million to reimburse the landlord for renovation costs due to budget constraints.” So the agencies sought it from the landlord, “due to the facility having no prior major renovations for cubicles.”

Auditors said that this line of defense — that the agency obtained the renovations through the lease because it didn’t have sufficient capital funds — “raises new concerns that the structure of this lease may have circumvented State budget law.”

Democratic Gov. Wes Moore’s administration has embraced leases, arguing that the state shouldn’t be saddled with large office buildings with potentially costly repair needs, with the example of the deteriorating State Center office complex in Baltimore looming large.

When it came to the Department of the Environment lease, auditors from the Department of Legislative Services noted that $7.9 million of the $10 million renovation budget “primarily consisted of cubicle enhancements.” And because the cubicle changes were not procured through a competitive bid, auditors could not determine whether the price was fair.

“DGS could not document that it assessed whether this work was necessary and that the costs were reasonable, or that it considered separately procuring the Services,” reads the audit.

The Department of General Services also could not show that it ever considered using furniture from the Maryland Correctional Enterprises, which sells a variety of products through a program that trains state inmates. State regulations “generally require agencies to procure goods and services from MCE when available,” the audit reads.

In its response, the department argued that the building’s owner Himmelrich Associates offered a plan to refurbish and renovate the existing cubicles” for the roughly 900-person agency “at a significant cost discount from purchasing new cubicles,” adding that cubicles from the correctional enterprise, on average, were “significantly” more expensive.

But auditors said the agency couldn’t show any documentation to prove that it assessed the cost of the correctional enterprise cubicles in advance, and the agency submitted “an email from June 2025, more than a year after the lease was awarded.”

Because furniture enhancements made up a majority of the costs, auditors argued that state officials “did not accurately represent” the deal when they brought it to the Board of Public Works, which ultimately approved it.

Before the Board, Maryland Secretary of the Environment Serena McIlwain praised environmental upgrades that were part of the lease, including a new solar panel array for the building and electrification upgrades. Board members, including Comptroller Brooke Lierman (D) and Moore echoed her praise.

But auditors found that the solar panel cost was actually included in the base rent, meaning the agency will pay for it over the 20-year term.

“Almost all the costs were unrelated to energy savings,” reads the audit.

In a response to auditors, the Department of General Services, led by Secretary Atif Chaudhry, argued that it didn’t mislead the Board by leaning on the energy-related upgrades, since the “summary of items listed in the agenda was meant to highlight the significant portions of the new renovation project,” whether they were paid for by base rent or the $10 million improvement allowance given to the agency.

Auditors also reviewed a similar 20-year lease for the Maryland Energy Administration, which is also headquartered at Montgomery Park. But they did not issue any findings specific to the Energy Administration.

Auditors also disputed the rental rate for the Department of the Environment’s space at Montgomery Park, which includes several floors in the historic building. Between the end of the agency’s previous lease at the building in 2022, and the start of its current lease, the rental rate climbed from $20.84 per square foot to $22.54 per square foot, an 8.2% jump, auditors wrote. That resulted in the $12.6 million increase in least costs, auditors wrote.

The Department of General Services, in its response to the audit, argued that the lease was in a two-year “holdover period” while the current lease was being negotiated, during which Himmelrich Associates would have received a 4% rate increase ($0.84 per square foot), had the original rate increase from the prior lease stayed in effect.

“DGS negotiated a rent increase of $1.65 per square foot and reduced the escalation rate from 4% to 3.45%,” reads the agency’s response.

The agency added that its real estate broker determined the fair market rental rate was $26.06 per square foot, on average.

The lease’s two-decade length, escalating 3.45% each year, also attracted scrutiny in the audit, which noted that the other leases auditors reviewed “were generally for 10-year terms and none of the escalation rates exceeded 3%,” though auditors noted that the agency did not have a policy setting maximum lease terms or escalation rates.

In response, the agency argued it had the freedom to negotiate a longer-than-usual term, and the agency “has seen similar requests and need for extended lease terms for larger leased space requirements.” But the agency noted that the renovation budget factored into the lengthy term, noting that “the landlord was unable to obtain financing to provide the $10 million renovation budget without a 20 year lease.”

According to the Department of General Services, the landlord also had issues financing the renovation effort if the state had the right to terminate the lease for “convenience,” or if cancellation was in the state’s best interest. The agency wrote that nixing the clause was the “only option,” to get the renovations, noting that the space hasn’t been renovated since 2002.

Auditors said that the department failed to show a good enough reason for excluding the clause, a common provision for state leases.

“The only documentation DGS provided to us was a letter from the landlord’s bank ‘respectfully requesting’ that the clause be removed from the lease agreement,” auditors wrote. “Given the length of the lease and the significant increase in the lease costs, we question whether the exclusion of this provision was in the State’s best interest.”
